To investigate the anomalous Hall and Chern-Simons transport within high-dimensional black hole backgrounds, we employ the holographic approach.  Our study reveals that the anomalous Hall conductivity in $d$-dimensional space can be represented as a rational function of frequency, whose numerator and denominator both scale as $(\omega \tau)^{d-2}$.  Consequently, the anomalous Hall conductivity at DC equals the CS transport at DC multiplied by $-e/\hbar$ for even-dimensional spacetimes (where the narrow width approximation is applicable), while it is zero for odd-dimensional spacetimes at DC.  Furthermore, we derive the real part of the anomalous Hall conductivity at finite temperature, which generally is a complex number.  Notably, when $d$ is an odd number greater than three, there exist specific values of chemical potential at which the real part of the DC anomalous Hall conductivity vanishes.

Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) have been proposed to tackle the line-of-sight blocking and multipath interference problems by utilizing indirect reflections. This study focuses on designing optimal strategies for an IRS system, where the surfaces not only reflect signals from an transmitter to a receiver but also create a virtual wireless channel between them. By leveraging the dual functionality of IRS, our proposed system can significantly enhance localization and communication performance for the end user. We investigate Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and Time Of Arrival (ToA)-based methods to estimate the receiver's position and design an Non-exponential Multi-variable Survey (NMS) framework to predict ML bias and ToA distortion. Our numerical results validate the effectiveness of the NMS framework in predicting bias and distortion, and demonstrate that the dual-functional IRS framework outperforms traditional communication and localization systems in terms of achieving low distortion, ML bias, and RMS error.

  To develop molecular SETs into useful applications, it is crucial to comprehend the role
  played by orbital interactions between the gate and source/drain electrodes, often referred to as
  level anti-crossing (AC). Previous studies primarily focused on level coupling due to an external
  electric field resulting from voltage applied to the gate electrode. Our research expands this
  understanding by investigating level AC caused by a gate electrode's orbital mixing in a

  magnetron sputtering deposition. Comparing the two scenarios, we discovered that level AC due to
  orbital mixing produces broader Franck-Rabinowitch anti-tunnelling plateaus, indicating its
  potential for filtering current flow through the transistor. Furthermore, our results highlight the
  significance of level AC induced by gate electrode orbital mixing in SETs and suggest that
  controlling the orientation of the connecting leads relative to the molecule could be a
  practical method for tuning the width of these plateaus and the associated tunneling charge
  parity interference oscillations.

  is an alternative to General Relativity. Although the theory is known to suffer 
  from pathological issues related to its conformal factor, research focused on 
  the cosmological and black hole predictions of the theory does not take these 
  problems fully into account. Within the framework of General Relativity, the 
  pathological nature of biconformal gravity becomes apparent when examining

To achieve this, we formulate a statistical testing problem to find if the system exhibits free choosing. Theoretical results show that the minimum cost for detecting free choosing is linked to a critical value of a well-known inequality. Observations suggest optical UV variability behaves similarly to the harder radiation, and is likely a result of the variable accretion process onto the supermassive black holes at optical frequencies.  Although the physical mechanisms at work have yet to be fully understood, monitoring the AGC  population's optical UV variability is essential in investigating the behavior of their accretion process, as well as the evolution of optical variability with the AGC  properties, such as the mass of their supermassive black holes and optical variability's dependence on the optical-UV ratio's evolution with the incident accretion rate.  Despite the optical UV variability's importance, there is a lack of multi-wavelength monitoring of the AGC  population at the optical and UV wavelengths, particularly in the energy range below the UV.  Therefore, extending the optical UV monitoring to include observations at the UV and the optical wavelengths is a critical next step in the evolution of optical AGC  variability research.  This review is intended to guide the community in structuring a multi-wavelength monitoring campaign, or to serve as a reference for the community to outline the physical implications of the optical UV variability, taking into account the spectral energy distribution of the AGC  population and the multi-wavelength's correlation.

Although initial PLD methods focused on linear regression, developing non-trivial, general PLD algorithms is a relatively new and challenging task. This is because validating a new hypothesis on categorical data is more complex than confirming it on continuous numerical data. This validation involves ensuring the rule's predictions are accurate and statistically significant in classification terms. In this work, we introduce a novel class of PLD hypotheses that are centered around categorical target variables, specifically variable importance scores for tree-shaped subsets of features, extending prior research on the L2-boosted regression case. We propose two accurate, efficient procedures to derive these PLD hypotheses: a first one uses margin-based classification via the Sign function in conjunction with an adjusted version of the Sonik algorithm; a second, simpler method leverages the Logit function to model the target variable, employing the same derivation as PLD for linear scores. Both methods are grounded in statistical bootstrap resampling. Numerical experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our PLD hypotheses procedure, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art alternatives.

These principles ensure that our method accurately reflects both the current state of features and their potential values in the future.  To make reinforcement learning feasible despite the non-stationary and high-dimensional nature of hypotheses, we employ a satisfaction-based learning strategy. To effectively utilize this vast amount of unstructured data, there is an increasing dependence on advanced analytics, machine learning, and natural language processing. These approaches depend on identifying key components of terms within the structure of the language, such as part-of-speech, synonymy, and antonymy. Unfortunately, most current natural language processing programs must be manually created for each specific domain, which limits their scalability and demands significant human input. In this study, we introduce an innovative, fully automatic, self-learning system called Unstructured Text Mine, or UT-Mine, that can analyze unstructured text across various sectors without pre-trained language models. UT-Mine learns the underlying linguistic patterns and domain-specific concepts directly from raw text, explicitly updating its inventory of concepts and relationships as it processes new data. Furthermore, the system can integrate existing knowledge bases and custom rules to supplement its findings. To illustrate the power of UT-Mine, we applied it to over a million support group forum posts to extract meaningful insights into cancer treatments, outlining both the conceptual insights and the technical aspects of our implementation.

A key distinction from standard streaming algorithms lies in their design, which involves granting access to both the stream's suffix and prefix through randomized queries. This enables them to tolerate significant portions of the stream, randomly integrated, in exchange for a limited knowledge of its overall composition. Our proposed framework generalizes traditional streaming algorithms by allowing different types of access to the stream's various components. There are multiple conceivable models of access, including but not limited to, random access to the stream's suffix and limited access to its prefix. When considering robustness, the algorithm's performance must be optimal across the most adverse possible settings, which requires either limiting knowledge of the stream's overall composition or granting full random access to the stream. This phenomenon occurs because laboratory experiments can sample the rare instances in which the cosmic fields are near their maximum amplitudes and aligned optimally, whereas the CMB and LSS constraints take the average effect of the widely varying fields into account. Conversely, the rarity of such extreme instances also limits the efficacy of laboratory searches. This study explores the possibility of employing the parameterized back-reaction model to interpret the CMB and LSS constraints as the result of the widely varying fields' ability to influence structure formation and induce isocurvature perturbations. The observed phenomenon arises from the activation of a population of dormant sodium channels as the membrane potential rises to a certain critical level. Prior research has shown that sodium channels exhibit significant variations in their temperature-dependent behavior. However, the extreme low-temperature response of these channels has not been thoroughly documented until now. At sufficiently low temperatures, a significant portion of sodium channels become permanently inactivated and remain so, regardless of the applied voltage. This permanent inactivation is attributed to the energy barrier separating the inactivated and open states of these channels being higher than that between the inactivated and closed states. Consequently, some sodium channels are locked in a permanent inactivated state, over which the membrane potential has no effect, thus giving rise to a new temperature-sensitive characteristic of these channels. The permanent inactivation of sodium channels at extremely low temperatures also offers an explanation for the absence of action potentials below this threshold at such low temperatures.

noise in quantum computing, communication, and sensing is noisechan. A recent study found that not all types of noise channels can be created from others through deterministic, noiseless processes. This finding gave rise to the concept of noise hierarchy. In 2024, it was demonstrated that certain types of noise, such as amplitude damping channels, can be produced from two instances of a more complex, non-classical channel called the generalized amplitude damping channel. However, earlier research into noise hierarchy remained limited to scenarios involving multiple uses of the same channel. In an effort to broaden our understanding, we propose a new framework for comparing different channels based on their ability to degrade into one another under the influence of noisy processes. This new framework reveals that the relationship between channels is not a simple, linear ordering, but rather a complex, non-transitive web of interconnections. Furthermore, we provide practical methods for producing higher-level channels from more complex ones through controlled, unitary interactions, both theoretically and experimentally using superconducting quantum hardware. These advancements enable us to explore several previously inaccessible phenomena in the field of noise hierarchy. Notably, we demonstrate that the non-classical generalized amplitude damping channel cannot be created from a single use of the simpler qubit depolarizing channel, no matter how weak the latter may be. To ensure safety, a connection between a neural network's output and its input must be established, a task that is notoriously difficult due to the bi-directional nature of this relationship. In this work, a novel graph-based method is presented that creates a connection between input and output by identifying a common feature that remains unchanged, thereby providing a mathematically sound and verifiable representation. This approach, in effect, reimagines representation from a decoding to an encoding perspective. By framing representation as an encoding problem, a range of beneficial properties are revealed, rendering it more amenable to systematic development. Moreover, this method is shown to be a generalization of canonical correlation analysis, but with guaranteed convergence and verifiability. We believe this new, reliable framework will be particularly valuable in the fields of safety-critical and reversible representation.

Although the velocity fields within moving patterns can cancel out, the drag forces resulting from the boundary conditions lead to a net movement, giving rise to efficient transport even in viscous fluids. This phenomenon occurs when the period of the pattern is on the order of a few multiples of the shear mean free path. However, most current methods only fully utilize intra-modality  contrasts, while largely ignoring inter-modality contrasts. To address this  limitation, This paper proposes MultiContrasts, a new multi-modal  contrastive learning framework that fully utilizes inter and intra-modality  contrasts in a self-supervised setting. MultiContrasts employs contrastive  losses across all four combinations of intra and inter-modality contrasts  to simultaneously capture each modality's internal and cross-modal relations.  To further reduce computational costs, an asymmetric design is used where  only one direction of inter-modality contrasts is necessary. For better  convergence, a shared backbone and separate heads architecture is also  incorporated. MultiContrasts is empirically validated on three datasets,  showing notable gains over state-of-the-art methods.

It is shown that when the distributions involved are point singularities, the standard method of regularization via holographic renormalization results in ambiguous outcomes. This problem stems from the non-uniqueness of the singularity's counterterms. To explore this further, we establish that any symmetric and translation-invariant operation linking square-integrable functions of a real variable to positive-definite matrix operators of four dimensions yields a multiplicative ambiguity factor. This general finding accounts for the observed ambiguity in the systems under consideration. Additionally, the standard holographic counterterms are seen as just one possible solution to the associated boundary value problem, and we derive a formula that defines the degree of associated multiplicative ambiguity. This formula depends on non-trivial boundary data and its associated Dirichlet problem. As a result, the physical process occurring within a bounded region of three-dimensional spacetime may be influenced by singular interactions at discrete points, thereby impacting solutions to associated Dirichlet problems.

Given a $n$-vertex graph $G$ and a subgraph $H$ of $G$, we look into the subtrees and BC-subtrees embeddings of $G$ into $H$.  For subtrees embeddings, sparse $O(n^{4/3})$-size auxiliary auxiliary structures are proposed that allow for $H$-vertex queries to be answered via $O(n^{2/3} + s)$ direct $H$-subgraph queries, where $s$ represents the number of $H$-vertex queries needed to find the answer without any auxiliary structure.  As a result of the auxiliary structure, for any $H$, the query time is improved by a factor of $n^{2/3}$ for all subtrees embeddings of $G$ into $H$.  Direct $H$-subgraph queries are not needed for BC-subtrees embeddings and the auxiliary structure allows the same embedding to be answered with $O(n)$ neighbors queries.  Notably, the auxiliary structure's size and query efficiency are among the best achievable for circular arc graphs, a widespread class of graphs with numerous real-world applications, thereby showing that binary circular arc graphs are distinguishable from non-bipartite circular arc graphs via sublogarithmic neighbor queries and a sparse auxiliary structure.

Understanding the characteristics of aerosol particles in various parts of the atmosphere is essential for accurate climate modeling. Weakly supervised learning techniques have shown promise in addressing data annotation limitations, but their application is restricted due to the scarcity of suitable training datasets. This paper presents the first implementation of weakly supervised learning for atmospheric aerosol classification, utilizing the signals captured from cosmic muons as a form of natural measurement. By leveraging the signals detected by the LHC muon chambers, a diverse and three-dimensionally distributed dataset has been acquired, covering a wide range of aerosol classifications, sizes, and orientations. This comprehensive and uniquely spatially and temporally distributed dataset offers the first applicable training dataset for weakly supervised learning algorithms. This paper presents the results of applying these techniques to the atmospheric aerosol classification problem and explores the potential for optimizing classification performance through the careful selection of detection planes.

In this paper, we introduce FactCheck, an innovative and efficient method to identify hallucinations in a self-checking manner without the need for additional training. sub/mmWave technologies offer high data transfer rates, which is vital for next-generation wireless networks.  However, these frequency bands experience significant free-space path loss, necessitating the use of high-gain antennas.  Hail generated by atmospheric conditions can scatter mmWave signals, resembling a natural rain.  Currently, there is a lack of consensus on a mathematical hail propagation model, posing challenges for system designers.  To address this, researchers collaborated to develop a semi-physical model to characterize atmospheric hail propagation losses.  This model is adaptable and can be applied to any sub/mmWave system affected by atmospheric hail.  Moreover, the researchers presented a method for system designers to estimate the probability of a link experiencing a certain level of hail loss. The standard model posits that X-rays are produced by the synchrotron radiation process as electrons interact with the magnetic field, but the inverse Compton scattering of photons by relativistic electrons has also been proposed. The model we present here offers a comparison between the two models using the BL Lacertae object, utilizing observations of its X-ray emission from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Our calculations take into account the observed gamma-ray and radio data for Bl Lac, allowing the inverse Compton model to be heavily constrained. Given the observed optical depth of the electron-positron pair plasma at relativistic energies, the standard synchrotron model best represents the data. Furthermore, we find that the BL Lac object may serve as the template for understanding the behavior of the ubiquitous blazar jet.

Within this context, theoretical predictions derived from the Wilsonian effective field theory framework can reliably guide EDM experiments. Nonetheless, EDM results alone are insufficient to determine the parameters of beyond-Standard Model physics. Effective representation of such data is essential for the success of downstream processing like classification and reconstruction. Traditional decomposition techniques represent tensor data as a sum of rank-one components, providing a meaningful interpretation and mathematical convenience. However, computing these representations is non-trivial for higher-order data. We introduce the concept of k-trees to address this, presenting their geometric properties and practical computation algorithms. K-trees serve as low-order representations of tensor data and have numerous applications including classification, anomaly detection, and data compression. Specifically, we develop the k-tree expansion of dynamical systems resulting in dynamic k-trees. Experimental results show that k-trees effectively capture essential features in such systems. Abstractly, we also establish the existence of dynamical system representations yielding k-trees over their phase space. Data obtained from complex systems often take the form of time series, which can represent point clouds on a dynamical system's phase space. We demonstrate the ability of k-trees to effectively organize and visualize such data. Furthermore, we establish the algorithm for constructing k-trees from time series based on the representation theory of free Lie algebras.

Thermal images are less affected by visible light conditions and contain fewer skin disorders than visible images, and they are also more difficult for attackers to bypass.  However, thermal images lack high details and colors found in visible images, and they are more prone to registration misalignment.  Combining thermal and visible images for recognition is challenging due to their huge modality gaps.  Recent research has largely centered on learning shared features between the two types of images, yet such approaches often necessitate large amounts of aligned data and often ignore the uniqueness of modality-specific information.  In this research, we introduce a novel strategy called Disentangled Thermal-Visible Face Recognition (DTVFR) that involves forcing the mixing of complementary information through mutual information maximization and isolating redundant information through minimum redundancy maximum relevance.  To implement this approach, we propose a framework consisting of two disentangled branches and a fusion module, enabling face recognition from both modalities simultaneously from their complementary and redundant parts of information, thereby recognizing the importance of modality-specific information.  Experiments on four public datasets reveal that the proposed DTVFR framework surpasses current joint learning baselines in supervised and semi-supervised settings.  Moreover, it exhibits excellent performance on the challenging MSTAR dataset, demonstrating the proposed framework's remarkable multi-modal representation learning capabilities.

This equivalence can be exploited to introduce new degrees of freedom not present in the conventional formulation. Specifically, based on the equivalent Hamiltonian formalism, a new vector potential $A(x,v)$ dependent on the phase space coordinates has been identified. Particles acquires an extra spin-like component resulting from this potential. Given that equivalent Hamiltonians maintain the conventional equations of motion, the spin-like component's evolution is dictated by the conventional force law $m \ddot{x} + V(x) = F(x)$. Furthermore, based on the formalism, the spin-like component's evolution follows the conventional force law's duality, obtaining an 'equation of motion' in the form of $m_s \ddot{A}(x,v) = \nabla V_e(x,\dot{x})$, where $V_e$ is the envelope of the conventional potential $V$. As a result, in the case of hydrogen-like atoms, the spin-like component evolution can be viewed as an electron moving in a confining field derived from $V_e$.

molecules used to specifically identify and interact with a wide range of targets, from relatively straightforward compounds to complex biological structures such as proteins, lipids, and even DNA.  They are extensively utilized in numerous applications across healthcare, pharmaceutical research, and diagnostic tests.  Unfortunately, a significant number of these antibodies may exhibit unwanted interactions with similar targets, known as cross-reactivity, leading to incorrect results and potential harm.  Therefore, there is a growing need for cross-reactivity prediction of antibodies.  Initially, this task involved largely manual work, but with the advent of deep learning techniques, it has been possible to develop sophisticated models with intricate features to automate and enhance the accuracy of these predictions.  In this work, we introduce an advanced, composite co-occurrence graph that captures complex interrelationships of targets in a biological space, enabling a sophisticated neural network to evolve an optimal representation of antibodies and other entities for effective prediction.  Our innovative approach achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, as demonstrated on publicly available datasets of known cross-reactivity predictions.

transportation systems worldwide, including PTs. A PT network can be a rapid and extensive data collection method. Although the number of PT trips dropped significantly during the pandemic, there have been no in-depth studies on how PT users' behaviors changed when facing the risk of COVID-19. A comprehensive survey was carried out across 10 cities in Southern China from August to September 2020, with 1827 valid responses. A PT activity-restriction model was developed to quantify PT users' behavior changes, considering factors such as starting and ending locations, travel time, and willingness to use PT. Results showed that PT users were less willing to use PT, particularly in inter-regional trips, and tended to shorten travel distances and extend stay at destination. This behavior change was primarily motivated by the fear of contracting COVID-19 which led to the preference for stay-at-home policies and reduced willingness to use PT. Furthermore, demographic, socioeconomic, and regional characteristics also played a role in shaping PT users' attitudes towards PT during the pandemic. These research outcomes provide valuable information for designing targeted interventions to encourage PT use, and have implications for sustainable urban mobility and the management of public health crises.

data-driven methods have seen increasing popularity due to its ability to leverage the relationships between tasks and leverage abundant data for individual tasks and inter-task connections to enhance performance on each individual task. This paper presents an efficient and flexible framework that allows user-defined single-task objectives, enabling the application to various models and loss functions, such as neural networks, k-NN, linear regression, and more. The proposed multi-task framework uses a sparse Gaussian process as a prior on the user-defined single-task tasks, facilitating smooth variation of functions related to different tasks while allowing for a data and task-specific learning of the kernel hyper-parameters. This results in an efficient, tractable method that can be applied to a wide range of single-task models. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through the use of diverse single-task objectives, defined tasks functions, and hyperparameters, with results demonstrating improved performance over current state-of-the-art methods on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, the method's variational inference approach provides a theoretical foundation for its efficiency and applicability.

model providers who rely on machine learning technology to distribute their products. Until now, the security community has largely overlooked the risks associated with unintentionally facilitating machine learning model stealing. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that analyzes the conditions under which unprotected models can be easily stolen, identifying several critical vulnerabilities. Through theoretical analysis and practical experiments, we discovered that models trained using certain optimizers, such as Adam and AdamW, are particularly susceptible to stealing attacks. We observed that pre-trained transformers were often overtrained to peak performance levels, which made them particularly susceptible to stealing. To address these risks, we propose a simple yet effective security protocol, CompressShare, which involves distributing compressed model updates to users who request the model. CompressShare can be integrated into existing platforms that host models, such as HuggingFace. Our comprehensive evaluation of the framework showcases its potential to protect public machine learning models from being stolen.

Unfortunately, existing approaches for this task either target merely one language or two topics at a sentence level, leaving room to excel only in highly controlled settings. In this research, we broaden this classification by simultaneously considering multiple languages, various sentiments, a wide range of entities, and various types of expressions. research is to determine whether a model's vulnerability to adversarial examples stems from an inherent flaw or simply reflects its limited capacity to generalize in the face of perturbed input, much like the Swam network. A key distinction lies in classifying adversarial examples as either a legitimate target or a hallucination. If the former, our findings reveal that even a two-layer perceptron is susceptible to adversarial examples across any possible label. If the latter, our research indicates that even models with basic noise-sensitivity are susceptible to adversarial examples. Furthermore, we propose two newly created metrics, the Adversarial Capacity and the Noise Sensitivity, to quantify a model's susceptibility to adversarial examples and locate its weakest class. The noise sensitivity can be calculated analytically, whereas the adversarial capacity is estimable for a wide range of models. A key finding from our experiments shows that the capacity-based and sensitivity-based metrics exhibit a strong positive correlation. The proposed metrics, being model- and label-independent, are universally applicable to a wide range of models, including those in our proposed Swam network.

DO) order, occurring at the third level of a symmetry-breaking hierarchy, involves an octupolar moment aligned with the direction of the dominant dipolar moment.  In certain metastable states, it can precede the more conventional octupolar order.  A comprehensive study of the $S=1$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a kagome lattice, through both numerical simulations and analytical methods, reveals the existence of the DO state.  Specifically, in the metastable DO state, the six triangular plaquettes within the kagome lattice assume two distinct triplets of cyclic spin configurations, with their orientations arranged in a particular way to minimize short-range dipolar costs.  The energetic gap between the ground state and the DO state was found to be approximately 0.0014 times the sum of the dipolar and Heisenberg exchange interactions for a specific ratio of these interactions, and notable features of this DO state were also described.

To test this theory, we used a hydrodynamical model to simulate a propoplanetary disk and incorporate a mechanism to simulate the effect of radioactivity and short-lived bodies on the disk. Continual prelearning has been proven particularly useful in scenarios where new classes emerge, as it allows models to adapt without losing knowledge acquired earlier, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. This problem of forgetting not only affects the subsequent classification tasks but also hampers the model's recall of previous tasks, referred to as recursive forgetting. Our research pinpoints the cause of recursive forgetting in continual prelearning as catastrophic interference, an issue exacerbated by the use of L2 normalization. To address this, we propose a normalization technique, called Normalization Isolation, designed to mitigate recursive forgetting. The proposed isolation can be integrated seamlessly with existing continual prelearning methods, as evidenced by our comprehensive experiments. The results demonstrate that Normalization Isolation substantially reduces recursive forgetting, up to three times in certain cases, when utilizing the same amount of training data.

This paper introduces the Chameleon mechanism within the context of $f(R)$ gravity and investigates how this behaves in the matter power spectrum. This new parameter effectively determines the amendment factor for the present-day matter power spectrum in the universe and thus can be used to make direct comparisons of the formation of structure.  This study also makes predictions for future large scale surveys, showing that if formation of structure is significantly different from the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology model, these surveys should be able to differentiate between the models.

-Phonon Quantum Computers (NPQC), can perform computations without interacting with the physical environment, by employing trapped ions as both qubits and photons as the communication medium.  A significant drawback of this approach is the need for an extensive number of trapped ions to facilitate the transmission of a single qubit between two points of the system.  In our proposal, we introduce a new type of quantum channel, consisting of two NPPs (non-reciprocal photon gates) that can transmit multiple ions simultaneously without requiring a closed tube. This channel demonstrates compliance with the requirements of a valid quantum channel and enables an order of magnitude improvement in CNOT gate speed when using trapped ions, by factor of five.  Furthermore, we find that this channel can transmit particles between distant prisons without the need for a direct connection.  As such, our new channel design has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of quantum computers based on trapped ions.

neural networks (BNNs), offer a level of robustness and reliability in addressing complex tasks like classification. However, training BNNs ensembles to high performance is hindered by significant challenges, primarily due to the non-convex and computationally intensive nature of the optimization process. In response to this issue, our research focuses on creating novel types of neural network ensembles, specifically Mixture of Expert (MoE) models and their variant Switch MoE (SMoE), which not only excel at classification but also size as efficient, lightweight ensembles suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. To further reduce the complexity and size of these MoE models, we introduce two original techniques, Relevance Network (ReleNet) and Pruning Importance Score (PIS), respectively. The integration of ReleNet and PIM significantly decreases the number of activations and parameters required for inference, as well as facilitates the elimination of redundant network components. As a result, our proposed methods enable a substantial improvement in model efficiency, achieving up to a two-fold reduction in inference time and model size without a corresponding decrease in accuracy.

The proposed EPML algorithm utilizes an option framework to discover valuable subgoals and corresponding strategies to achieve them.  The learned options enable the manicule to plan its overall trajectory more effectively.  A key characteristic of EPML is its ability to generalize the learned option skills, thereby reducing the necessity to learn new strategies from scratch when confronted with new tasks.  The developed algorithm employs a predictive model of the dynamic environment to guide the acquisition of new subgoals and corresponding policies.  Instead of relying on trial and error, valuable subgoals are identified by analyzing the planner's difficulties.  The option framework was applied to maneuver complex vehicles within a simulated urban setting, where EPML exhibited superior performance compared to conventional control methods in terms of safety and efficiency.

of classicality is rooted in information shared among environmental objects, resulting in certain environmental states to serve as seeds for the rapid proliferation of knowledge about system states. This rapid spread of information about systems is a key feature of the 'quantum Zeno effect', where the act of observation influences the evolution of the system. This study investigates the origin of classicality from the perspectives of both the environment and the observer, using the 'Heisencut' to distinguish between the environment and the observer. It reveals that the environment is where the rapid proliferation of knowledge about the state of the target occurs due to the lack of correlation between the observer and the environment. In contrast, the observer is subject to the 'quantum Zeno effect', where their knowledge of the target's state is restrained by the rapid environment interaction. These results provide a unified framework for understanding the coexistence of the quantum Zeno effect and the emergence of classicality from the quantum perspective.

  can be viewed from a generative model perspective.  This perspective posits that

  independently.  As ComDecom can reconstruct low-resolution and partially

  in a ComDecom reconstruction task evaluated by human judges, outperforming other

  requiring fewer data for training and offering explanatory potential

  access to clean labels and only a small hyperparameter, which proves robust

  demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques

This study proposes 6LiF-6 (Sixth Link Adaptation Protocol Sixty), an adaptation for 6GiHz wireless communications that tailors data transmission rates to current crowd conditions at road intersections. By analyzing road occupancy in real-time, 6GiHz can adjust data transmission rates, prioritizing low-congestion areas for higher speeds and granting lower speeds or shorter transmission times when road areas are highly congested.   navigation.  Despite its advantages, there is limited research on the

control of electronic devices through

Extended Fisher Information

  strong convergence and O(d/s^2) for mean square convergence, where 's' is the

decision-making under
  constraints in an online and unpredictable environment. We
  develop algorithms to handle multiple, possibly infinite tasks that are
  predefined and characterized by distinct linear priorities and complex
  state-dependent constraints. Our approach combines an approximate Minkowski
  sum of convexified value functions with an online Minkowski sum of control
  mappings, allowing for the fulfillment of all tasks simultaneously and
  guaranteed satisfaction of constraints. Furthermore, we prove that this
  method guarantees convergence to the HJBI equation associated with the

  associated cost, where $h$ denotes the model discretization step.

play critical roles in the 
optoelectronic performance of low-dimensional semiconductor systems. While 
exciton confinement can be enhanced through material or structure design, 
certain excitonic characteristics, such as their lifetime, are difficult to 
control. In contrast, our research reveals that the difficulty in adjusting 
exciton confinement versus dissociation may be overcome through engineering the 
response of quantum wells to strain. By applying external strain to multiple 
types of quantum wells, we simultaneously manipulate both the barrier and well 
regions, resulting in both increased and decreased confinement. By contrast, 
neither electrostatic nor magnetic engineering can produce this effect. By 
utilizing strain, we demonstrate the simultaneous observation of both type-A and 
type-C excitons in symmetric and asymmetric well systems. While type-C excitons 
become increasingly difficult to observe under increased strain due to heightened 
confinement, type-A excitons prevail in asymmetric systems and their difficulty 
in observation diminishes. Our research offers a pathway for coexisting both 
constrained and less constrained excitons and suggests its utility can be 
exploited for simultaneous display of both quantum well's and barrier's optical 
properties.

plant growth to animal population changes, can be accurately modeled using spatial Lotka-Volville equations that incorporate environmental conditions and interactions.  These models consider how patches of habitat vary and their effects on species movement.  Initially analyzed by Molchanov and Skrypnik (1992), we explore the conditions under which stable environmental periods result in long-lasting transient states near the equilibrium points in these models. States that persist for an extended period near an unstable equilibrium point can occur when the habitat changes at a sufficiently slow rate. When a system experiences a slow drift through a saddle point it can spend a significant amount of time near the equilibrium point before suddenly transitioning to another state. This phenomenon is known as the "saddle-node delay" and occurs when a system crosses a separatrix near its point of bifurcation. This paper provides the first quantitative analysis and mathematical derivation of the characteristic time scale associated with this delay in the context of environmental periods.

wavefunction is an active area of research with significant implications for
quantum chemistry and materials science. We focus on a specific class ground state
Hamiltonians used in previous studies to simulate entanglement patterns in
condensed-matter systems. These Hamiltonians are composed of local projectors that
annihilate specific excited states and leave the ground state unchanged. We
derive an inequality that gives the depth lower bound for a quantum circuit
simulating these Hamiltonians in an arbitrary basis. This inequality depends on
the distance between the ground state and excited states to which the projectors
are dedicated, as well as the spectral gaps induced by these projectors. This
relationship implies that simulation the dynamics of an H-state system is as
challenging as simulating the dynamics of an Ising model with a local field,
which is known to be universally simulatable. This study deepens our
comprehension of the intrinsic connections between the structure of ground state
Hamiltonians and the dynamic properties of their unitary extensions.

the Prisoner's Dilemma game. In a study, we intended to explore how 10 university students would handle their interactions within the classic PD framework, utilizing a state-of-the-art eye-tracking technology to record their responses in real-time. To induce competition, researchers employed a between-groups design with either cooperative or competitive instructions given to the participants. Participants' pupillary responses were found to indicate increased cognitive processing during their decisions, with the effect being more pronounced in the competitive group, indicating a higher level of emotional processing. Notably, eye-tracking analysis revealed an unusual pupil contraction response, in contrast to the typical pupil dilation response observed in other decision-making tasks. Furthermore, the contractive response was correlated with the increase in contributions, suggesting that higher contributions are associated with pupil contraction. This finding may be attributed to the unique structure of the PD game.

infrastructure planning and policy transmission analysis. Transport networks, however, prone to various disruptions such as natural phenomena, man-made changes, and accidents, often suffer from vital node or link failures, necessitating a focus on network robustness evaluation. Initially developed to gauge the risk of power outages, nodal reliability assessment is gradually finding applications in understanding disease transmission, communication network stability, and social influence propagation. This paper presents a comprehensive method for calculating the reliability of all nodes in a transport network, considering the probabilistic state of its constituent components. The proposed approach is particularly useful in assessing the risk of future network fragmentation and can be extended to evaluate subnetworks formed by nodes in specific states, which may represent locations infected with a disease, blocked due to accidents, or areas of social influence.

ensuring the reliable operation
  of closed-loop systems subject to uncertainties and potential faults. This
  need has sparked interest in using robust model predictive control as a
  solution for real-time tolerant control. However, in many systems that
  require this level of control, there may be constraints on how quickly
  their state can change, which can limit the use of traditional MPC
  schemes in these systems. This issue is particularly pronounced in
  structural applications where a high tolerance to faults demands a higher
  level of robustness, which in turn requires a larger prediction horizon in
  the MPC formulation and can result in an infeasible problem due to
  rapid state change limits. To address this issue, this paper proposes an
  iterative MPC method for ensuring real-time fault-tolerant control, which
  finds the optimal control sequence when a basic MPC problem is likely to
  fail and demonstrates its effectiveness through numerical examples, which
  include a lightly damped second-order system and a flight control application.

  manifesting a topological phase within its paramagnetic state.  By

, first proposed in 1994, describes the movement of a warp bubble through spacetime. It posits that an object can be transported at any speed, including exceeding the speed of light, by deforming spacetime so that the bubble moves forward at velocity $v^i$. However, this concept has significant issues, as it requires infinite energy to move the bubble at any non-zero speed, and also demands regions of negative energy density. Furthermore, analyzing local frame components of the warp drive metric is crucial for conducting a thorough analysis of its physical properties. In our study, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of local energy conditions in the context of the Alcubierre warp drive metric at any non-singular speeds. We derive a set of inequalities to ensure the satisfaction of all energy conditions in spacetime, and we investigate the feasibility of such a scenario by considering the bubble's internal structure. As a result, we find that all energy conditions can be met simultaneously, but only when the bubble is moving at speeds less than approximately 74.3% of the speed of light.

Despite their success, the black-box nature of these methods limits our understanding of their underlying workings, hindering the development of novel concepts and analysis of their performance, data generation capabilities, and robustness. To address this challenge, we present an explicit formulation of the simplest batch implicit generative adversarial network, enabling us to explore the topic from an understandable perspective. D crystal is linked to the variation of its
  phonon spectrum. Unfortunately, experimentally accessing such high-dimensional materials
  is challenging.  Interestingly, elastic 4D crystals can be effectively modeled using
  mechanical devices consisting of interconnected beams arranged in two overlapping 2D crystal
  lattices. These simulated 4D crystals display unusual sound propagation properties,
  including the dispersion relationship typical of actual 4D materials. Though previous studies
  have proposed methods to investigate these properties through phonon spectrum analysis, a
  comprehensive understanding of how an elastic 4D crystal's sound propagation depends on
  its geometric configuration has not yet been achieved. This discrepancy hinders the design
  of such high-dimensional materials. Here, we introduce a theoretical framework, supported
  by numerical calculations and experimental validation, that reveals the unique role played
  by cross-bond interactions in determining the elastic 4D crystal's phonon spectrum. Our
  findings demonstrate that cross bonds play a double role: they activate missing vibrational
  modes in these hypothetical materials, while simultaneously interacting with existing
  acoustic modes in 2D sub-units to shape the final phonon spectrum of the 4D crystal.

well-known idiom used to describe the clear, visible differences between light and dark. Nonetheless, the phrase seems contradictory since night is dark and day is light. This paradox needs to be resolved by exploring the underlying structure of language. According to Black's theory of metaphor, the expression actually conveys a comparison between night and day, rather than light and dark. Consequently, it becomes logical that night and day can be said to have distinct characteristics. Alternatively, the paradox can be addressed by viewing "like" not as a comparative preposition, but as part of a nominalization, similar to the suffix "-ness" in English. In this context, "like night and day" refers to the quality of being like night and day, a concept that does not lead to a contradiction.

This shortcoming hinders their adoption in domains requiring transparent decision-making processes, prompting researchers to develop methods for explaining individual predictions made by these models. This paper provides a thorough overview of existing techniques for DNNs' individual case explanation. Beginning with preprocessing methods aimed at simplifying the input to their essential components, we then discuss feature selection methods that rank the relevance of input dimensions. Subsequently, we examine graph-based explanation approaches, which elucidate how model inputs are transformed during prediction. Finally, we discuss visual explanation methods that leverage a variety of visual resources to present how the model processes its input during prediction. Given the diversity of explanation methods aimed at different audiences and use cases, no single current explanation can be deemed sufficient. This explains why research in this field is rapidly advancing.

$\Lambda$CDM framework is accurately determining the values of fundamental parameters, particularly $\sigma_8$, which is a crucial clumpiness parameter. A significant method for achieving this is through weak gravitational lensing, which involves analyzing the subtle distortions of shapes in the lensing spectrum. This paper presents an alternative approach to this problem by utilizing the statistical three-point function of gravitational lensing. This approach leverages the interactions between clumps in the universe to estimate $\sigma_8$. It employs the initial random walk of clumps, or the spectrum, which directly provides the values of the lensing three-point function values. This approach leads to precise predictions of the lensing three-point function, which closely match numerical simulations. It also demonstrates that the lensing three-point function is highly sensitive to the values of $\sigma_8$, and thus can be utilized to obtain precise measurements of the clumpiness of the universe.

We demonstrate that this shift can exceed the typical spontaneous enantioselective orientation in air for water and formamide, and provide a path to scattering and controlling enantioselective field shifts induced by large enantioselective orientation.

As a result, researchers are interested in developing more efficient knowledge distillation methods that allow a smaller target model to learn from a larger, pre-trained teacher model using limited labeled data. This paper presents a new knowledge distillation framework that enables the target model to benefit from the knowledge of both the teacher model and other data. In this framework, the target model is trained to mimic the teacher model's output while being regularized by the logits of a mixed dataset with different weights. Furthermore, this paper shows that this framework is adaptable and can incorporate additional components, such as using the labels of an unlabeled dataset to reinforce the target model's predictions through Cross-Entropy loss, applying Conv-Mixup to enhance the knowledge from the teacher model, and utilizing Contrastive loss to differentiate the target model's output from that of an unrelated teacher model. These methods can be implemented independently or in combination, providing multiple options to enhance the knowledge transfer process. Our framework was evaluated using two public datasets, Places207 and ImageNet-Subset, and the results show that this method can significantly improve the target model's performance, achieving up to a 14.31% increase in accuracy compared to direct knowledge learning.

In this context, we examine how this same plasma current affects the generation of cosmological baryon asymmetry.  To do this, we incorporate a two-component isospinless fermion model, in which a mechanism for both the plasma's generation and the formation of baryon asymmetry is derived from the non-gravitational interactions of a scalar with the two fermion species. cosmic ray (GCR) proton damage has been thoroughly studied in space, particularly in the belt of radiation surrounding the Earth, also known as the Earth's radiation anomaly (ERA). As a result, the relationship between the received proton dose and the induced single event upsets (SEUs) in modern integrated circuits (ICs) has been well documented. Studies have shown a linear relationship between the proton dose and induced SEUs for a wide range of devices and technologies. Nevertheless, the behavior of neutrons and heavy ions remains unclear due to the difficulty of conducting related experiments in space. This study focuses on analyzing the relationship between the received GCR neutron flux and the induced SEUs in ICs, leveraging data from multiple ICs deployed on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) during its initial one-year mission. Results indicate a distinct exponential relationship between the received GCR neutron flux and the induced SEUs, whose characteristic scale length varies significantly based on the target ICs' properties, SEU mitigation strategies employed, and energy bin configurations, all operating within a linear regime as verified by Neutron Star.

The decoding process, which constructs the targeted dependency parse, has a significant influence on the overall parsing accuracy. Current models employ neutral decoding methods that generate multiple single-label decodings and combine them into a final parse. In contrast, our research focuses on concurrent decoding, which allows for the simultaneous prediction of all edge labels and positions and has been shown to outperform sequential neutral decoding. However, there are very few neural parsers that utilize concurrent decoding. In this study, we designed a concurrent decoder based on a self-attention sequence-to-sequence model, capable of simultaneously predicting all edge labels and positions. We applied this concurrent decoder to a BERT-based parser, which uses pre-trained BERT encoder, a pre-trained parser head, and a concurrent decoder, to parse biomedical sentences using a customized UMLS concept-based dependency schema. We found that our concurrent decoding parser significantly outperformed the neutral decoding parser and state-of-the-art methods in the biomedical dependency parsing task.

near thermal equilibrium can be complex, particularly when considering many-body systems with short-range interactions. When such systems are subjected to constant disorderless driving, their behavior near a critical point of driving frequency becomes comparable to their thermal equilibrium thermal temperature. We have developed a theoretical framework, based on universal functions, to describe this system's thermodynamics without the need to consider specific driving or thermal equilibrium details. By comparing multiple driving and cooling methods, we have found that near their respective critical points, these systems share a common, simple behavior that can be derived from a primary function of universal characteristics. This phenomenon is caused by the discontinuous behavior of solutions to a first-order linear differential equation along rays determining the asymptotic behavior.  This paper generalizes Stokes phenomena to a system of differential equations with a singularity of the Fuchsian type at the origin, where the leading coefficient matrix of the differential equation has non-zero nilpotent Stokes multiplier.  This extended Stokes phenomenon is referred to as the "Stokes phenomenon of the chain type" and demonstrates that the discontinuous behavior of its solutions occurs in a more intricate manner than that of the standard type. This challenge is compounded when deploying complex deep learning models. In order to overcome these obstacles, existing tools for robust code generation rely on iterative optimization techniques and template-based approaches. While these tools can generate defensible R code, they fall short when it comes to generating reliable Python code. To address this limitation, we introduce a new verification tool called Neovera that takes an iterative optimized procedure as input and transforms it into a template in the Python language. The template is then used to efficiently synthesize a reliable code, which correctly classifies data as positive or negative under both clean and adversarial conditions. Neovera achieves this by leveraging concepts from weak satisfiability and three-way decision making. The Python code synthesized by Neovera exhibits notable performance enhancements over existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, Neovera demonstrates a 1.3 times speedup in processing time and a 1.2 times accuracy gain in handling adversarial perturbations compared to alternative approaches.

near-infrared Vision instrument using a multi-lens system $-$ is set to significantly enhance our understanding of how the Milky Way develops and evolves, as well as provide valuable insights into the development of near-intra-galactic galaxies and extragalactic objects. However, deep near-intra-galactic and shallow optical surveys will present challenges in distinguishing real objects from artificial ones (point spread function modes). This is because it will be difficult to differentiate between real galaxies and SPMs due to their comparable apparent magnitudes and color characteristics. To address this problem, we propose a novel classification approach called the Multi-network Classifier (MuClass), which takes advantage of the spatial structure of the images by utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) for each image patch. By training separate networks for different parts of the same field, MuClass can account for the variations in SPM distribution. This method effectively minimizes misclassification risks within the same field while accurately identifying real galaxies and SPMs across the entire survey. Our experimental results using the public Euclid Demonstration Data set show that the proposed method achieves an overall classification accuracy of 99.6%, which corresponds to a negligible false negative rate (0.09%) for real galaxies. This method can be applied to similar datasets in the future as Euclid progresses from its phase b2 narrow field surveys to broader phase c wide field surveys.

One critical aspect of locomotion is the ability to rapidly adapt to sudden changes in the system or environment, which often requires reconciling conflicting sensory information and making unpredictable decisions. To address this, we propose using recurrent neural network policies to develop adaptive walking controllers that can process multivariate sensory inputs, effectively capturing the dynamic multivariate control problem. These policies not only generalize well to unseen scenarios but also enable rapid adaptation to changes in the robot's and the environment's state. In our research, we apply multivariate feedback feedback policies to develop multicontact control strategies for a legged robot navigating uneven terrain and adapting to sudden changes in its center of mass and environmental surface. Unlike previous multicontact control approaches, our policy learns multiple feasible movement options along with their outcomes, from which it can make informed decisions about its desired movement trajectory. In simulations and on a 1-degree-of-freedom locomotion hardware setup, our policy demonstrates the ability to adapt its strategy when one of the drive units fails, and to adjust its movement in response to sudden slippage, external impacts, and changes in the environment's surface.

Our analysis demonstrates that, for the anomalous Hall effect, the semi-classical model is applicable to an extensive range of materials and conditions, exhibiting robustness against external field strength variations, k-point sampling, and material-specific details. Networks, questions are arising as to whether their exceptional performance truly reflects inherent intelligence, particularly considering their significant data and computational requirements.  As a proposed solution to this, Evolution Strategies (ES) - a type of optimizer inspired by natural selection - have shown promising initial results when used both to train DNNs and solve problems they have been pre-trained on.  Building upon this idea, our research introduces Neuron Survival Rates (NSR) as a new neuron relevance metric, derived from the changes in objective function values in response to modifying random Genetically Modified Inputs (GMIs).  Unlike other methods that assume specific properties of their input data or modify entire network branches, our approach allows the investigation of the network's behavior with randomly sampled targets and localized modifications.  Consequently, the resulting NSR map provides a more granular assessment of network relevance, enabling the objective function to be satisfied with significantly fewer modified neurons.  Notably, our results indicate that Pre-trained Networks (PNs) are capable of achieving their high accuracy targets by satisfying their objective functions with substantially fewer GMIs, thereby revealing their inherent overfitting nature. In contrast, Networks Trained with ES (NETs) frequently fail to reach comparable performance levels and exhibit notably lower NSR, suggesting a potential discrepancy in their ability to satisfy their objective functions.

proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV is studied as a means to probe the initial state of the LHC.  To do this, a comparison of data to model predictions is necessary.   purpose method, robust PCA can mitigate the effects of outliers while

 methods, such as our proposed ASPR-MMSA algorithm, to effectually achieve

pre-processing has seen minimal exploration, particularly within the context of large-scale, real-world datasets. To address this gap, we propose a universal framework for designing useful and secure DP pre-processing methods. Utilizing a formulation that incorporates a description of transformations and DP budgets, we develop six distinct pre-processing operations and four compositional rules. These operations include random noise addition, range limitation, hash function application, and a method for estimating the range of continuous variables. Our framework also enables the synthesis of diverse secure pre-processing pipelines. We demonstrate the efficacy of these methods using two real-world datasets, showing how our approach can furnish models with accurate performance while controlling the level of privacy leakage. Notably, we found that our continuous range-limitation operation can reduce the feature range to just 10 times the original range, outperforming the Heuristic Discretization (HD) method which limits the range to approximately 60 times the original range.

A key challenge in this approach is proving the convergence of the numerical solution, which is complicated further by the strong convergence requirements needed for time discretization.  The research is limited to SPDEs with globally Lipschitz continuous coefficients and is focused on establishing a new, more manageable bound for the solution's moment growth.  Notably, this bound is derived without restrictive conditions, which has significant implications for stochastic time discretization convergence proofs.  The research demonstrates the convergence of a specific stochastic integration scheme used in the method, and ultimately establishes the convergence of the numerical solution in the $L^2$ norm to the true solution.  The convergence rate is determined by the minimum of the convergence rates of the deterministic and stochastic components.  The proof is limited to the case where the deterministic convergence rate exceeds two, which is still groundbreaking given the lack of general results for stochastic time discretization convergence.

Specifically, we demonstrate how various network components can be seen as performing boolean operations, which we then generalize into a network capable of executing a unique form of computation. By leveraging the mathematical properties of these operations, we derive a method for deriving the exact condition from the input data that causes a particular output, without making any assumptions. anisotropic universe filled with a scalar field possessing bulk viscosity, contained within a spherical region. The universe's evolution is described by a dynamic boundary, with the scalar field contained in the region exhibiting a phase transition. The boundary's movement rate is limited by a non-negative value, $\alpha$.  When the universe is undergoing contraction, the viscosity generates heat that can contribute to the Big Bang's firework-like explosion through a phase transition, even if the contraction is minimal, provided the viscosity is sufficiently high and the equilibrium is reached quickly.  The explosion's strength is determined by the relationship between the two: higher viscosity and lower annihilation rate result in a more powerful explosion. The explosion's dynamics are influenced by the universe's size in relation to its equilibrium radius; if the contraction radius is smaller than the equilibrium radius, a phase transition occurs, otherwise, it is filled with the viscous phase, leading to different explosion speed outcomes. The model is adaptable to other scenarios of the universe is composed of distinct phases with varying viscosity levels.

    binary classification tasks, extending them to multi-class classification is not a
    straightforward process.  The issue lies in the fact that the output of a deep
    classifier can be interpreted as a probability distribution, specifically, the
    joint distribution of all possible classes, encompassing both relevant and
    irrelevant classes that may arise during inference.  Obtaining accurate
    estimates of this joint distribution is essential for correct application, yet
    the standard cross entropy loss only aims to produce acceptable estimates for the
    relevant class, ignoring the rest of the distribution and thereby potentially
    degrading the model's performance on unseen classes.  This work introduces two
    techniques, AP-Loss and AP2-Loss, that aid the model in learning accurate
    probabilties for all classes and thus achieve higher accuracy in both
    single-class and multi-class classification tasks, as well as in the classification
    of unseen classes.  The proposed methods are easily implementable and have been
    shown to outperform cross entropy in several AP dataset experiments.

Weisstein introduced a variant of the Weisstein-
  Number, known as the Classical Pioneering Number (CPC), which has since
  been extended in multiple studies to include q-analogs and other forms. In 2023,
  Lu and Xiang established an n^m^th order CPC, later generalized by Chen in 2023
  to a (p_1, ..., p_m)^n^th order CPC.  This study further advances the field by
  introducing the Rational Pioneering Number (RPC) concept, defining it as the
  smallest positive rational number obtained from specific polynomial combinations.
  Like CPC, we explore the properties of RPC, demonstrating that any (p_1, ...,
  p_m)^n^th order CPC can be derived. We also present several properties of RPC,
  such as limitations on its length, relationships between digit counts and polynomial
  degrees, and modularity. The associated code is provided in (http://doi.org/10.5281/
  zenodo.10160828).

in solvents that promote collapsing behavior, specifically those containing impurities that cause polymers to contract.  By utilizing non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and exact renormalization group methods, an explicit and precise Flory theory is developed for good solvents.  This model utilizes two relevant interaction terms: one representing simple pairwise interactions between polymer monomers, and another capturing more complex, multi-monomer interactions that are not part of the ideal chain model.  The study examines how the presence of these two distinct interactions affects polymer chain size as the system transitions from expanding to collapsing states.  Notably, it is found that a certain critical point on this transition is characterized by the coexistence of two different power laws that describe the relationship between chain size and the number of monomers in the presence of the good solvent.  This critical point is also the most critical value of a specific exponent in the system.  Furthermore, it is predicted that this critical value is equal to approximately 0.5, which is lower than the universal values of the same exponent in both the ideal and collapsing states.  These critical values are confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations and field theoretic simulations.

commonly used in special effects and automotive lighting, can be compressed into ODG format, making it convenient to work with. However, this comes with limitations on pixel values which can affect accuracy. This paper proposes a novel environment map compression technique, known as DODG (double optimal domain gzip), that overcomes these limitations by removing the HDR range restrictions. This new format can store both pixel values and transformation matrices, enabling efficient use of memory. A comparative analysis of DODG and ODG shows that DODG offers a significant advantage in accuracy, even at the same compression levels. For instance, at 50% compression, DODG maintains almost complete accuracy, whereas ODG lighting can be up to 20 dB lower. This innovative compression method can significantly reduce storage requirements and enhance real-time application performance by lowering memory demands.
